questions.q: Why can a randomized A/B test support a causal claim when an observational comparison often cannot?
options: Because it uses more data
Because random assignment makes the groups comparable in everything except the change being tested
Because the p-value is always smaller
Because it avoids using a control group
questions.explain: Chance alone decides who gets the treatment, so confounders are balanced on average across groups. Any systematic difference in outcome can be attributed to the change.

questions.q: Which items should be decided BEFORE launching the experiment?
options: The winning variant and the final p-value
Which of many metrics looks best
The primary metric, randomization unit, alpha, power, minimum detectable effect, and sample size
Whether to stop early if the result looks good
questions.explain: Fixing the metric, error rates, MDE, and sample size in advance prevents metric-fishing and early stopping from inflating false positives.

questions.q: In the lesson, detecting a lift from 10% to 12% at alpha 0.05 and 80% power needed about 3,841 users per group. What happens to the required sample if you want to detect a much smaller lift, such as 10% to 11%?
options: It stays about the same
It gets smaller
It rises sharply, to about 14,751 per group
It becomes exactly double
questions.explain: The required sample size scales with one over the squared effect, so detecting smaller effects takes many more users.

questions.q: What does 80% statistical power mean for the designed test?
options: If a real effect of the minimum detectable size exists, the test will detect it about 80% of the time
The result will be correct 80% of the time
There is an 80% chance the null hypothesis is true
80% of users will see the new variant
questions.explain: Power is the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when the true effect is the size you planned for.

questions.q: You run an A/A test where both groups get the identical experience. Roughly what fraction of runs should come out significant at alpha 0.05?
options: About 80 percent
None of them
About 50 percent
About 5 percent
questions.explain: With no true difference, the false positive rate is alpha, about 5 percent. A much different rate on live traffic suggests broken randomization or tracking.
